body.p: ArraysEntries Array. A unit in the index consisting of all the entries common to the same main heading. Sometimes also called an entry.

Blind cross-references Blind cross-reference. A cross-reference that does not lead anywhere in the index; for instance, in an index with no array for “Dogs,” a cross-reference saying “Canines. See Dogs.”
Circular cross-references Circular cross-reference. A set of cross-references that lead the user in a never-ending circle (Books. See Texts; Texts. See Documentation; Documentation. See Books).
Continued line. An abbreviated version of the heading, followed by an abbreviation for the word “continued,” repeated at the top of a new column when an array runs over more than one column.
Cross-references Cross-reference. Provides a navigational structure that helps guide users from one place in the index to another. There are two types: see also references and see references.
Depth of indexing GranularityDepth of indexing Depth of indexing (granularity). The level of detail in the text that will be picked up in the index.
Disambiguation Disambiguation. The art of distinguishing two identical terms with different meanings, usually with a parenthetical comment (Henry IV (king of England); Henry IV (king of France)).
Double-posting Double-posting. The placement of identical locators under two or more different headings, allowing users to find the information they want in whichever of those places they look.
Embedded indexing Embedded indexing. The tagging of entries and/or text so that entries may be attached, or embedded, into the text itself and the locators generated when the book is formatted.
Entriesdefinition Entry. The atom of the index; consists of a piece of information and its location in the text.
Exhaustivity Exhaustivity. Inclusion of all relevant material in the index. Exhaustivity must go hand-in-hand with discrimination.
Headingsdefinition Heading. The terms in the index that lead the user to information.
Headnotes Headnote. Placed at the beginning of the index, a set of instructions to readers, alerting them to any unusual or nonstandard practices in the index.
Indented style Indented style. A format for presenting index entries in which each subhead is set off individually, on its own line.
Inversion Inversion. Flipping the order of words in a phrase for alphabetizing purposes (Malpractice, medical).
Locatorsdefinition Locator. The part of the entry that tells readers where the information in the heading is located in the text.
Metatopic Metatopic. The overarching subject that the book is about.
Orphan (indexing) Orphan. The last line of an entry as the first line of a page or column.
Run-in style Run-in style (paragraph style). A format for presenting index entries in which subentries are joined after the main heading on a continuous line.
Subheadingsdefinition Subheading (or subentry). Secondary levels of information in an array, providing more detailed information about the main heading.
Undifferentiated locators Undifferentiated locators. Multiple locators attached to a heading.
Wrapped lineRunover line Runover line Wrapped line. See Runover line. A continuing, usually indented line that is used for an entry that is too long to fit on a single line.
